title: Should a client build, partner or buy to get into a new market?
description: Build, partner or buy? for case interviews. How to get into a new market or capability. A checklist, a worked example and how to say it.
hook: A client can get into a new market or capability in three ways: build it, partner for it or buy it. Choose by asking how fast it is needed, how much control the client wants, what each route costs over the same time period, and whether the client can actually carry it out.
body:
When it helps

Use this after you have decided the client should do something new, as the "how" step of a market entry or growth case. It also tests the alternatives branch of an acquisition case: could the client get the same benefit without buying?

The comparison

RouteGood becauseWatch out for
Build (organic)Full control; no integration or culture clashSlow; needs skills the client may not have
Partner (joint venture, alliance, licence)Shared risk and cost; fast accessShared control and profit; partner may become a rival
Buy (acquire)Fastest; brings customers and skillsExpensive; integration and culture risk

An example: a supermarket adds pharmacies

A UK supermarket wants to offer pharmacy services. Build: hire pharmacists and fit out counters, which is slow but gives full control. Partner: let an existing pharmacy chain run counters inside its stores, which is fast and low risk but shares the profit. Buy: acquire a pharmacy chain, which is fastest but expensive and hard to integrate. The best route depends on how fast the supermarket needs it and how much it wants to own the customer relationship.

Compare costs over the same period

An illustrative retailer needs a product recommendation engine within twelve months.

  • Build: $2.5M upfront plus $600,000 a year to run. Over three years: $2.5M + 3 × $0.6M = $4.3M.
  • Partner: a vendor charges $1M a year plus implementation. Over three years: $3M plus implementation, but the vendor controls the data and the features.
  • Buy: a specialist firm costs $8M plus integration.

The $8M is not a three-year expense like the others. It buys a business that still has value after three years and could be sold again, so compare it on value, not cost alone.

Then apply the deadline. If building takes two years, it fails the twelve-month requirement however cheap it is. That leaves partner or buy, and the deciding question is whether recommendations will be a source of advantage. If yes, owning the capability matters and buying looks better. If no, partnering is cheaper and faster.

How it sounds in an interview

"There are three ways in: build it, partner for it or buy it. I'd choose based on speed, cost and how much control we need. Can I check how quickly the client wants this, and whether this capability is core to how it competes?"

The weak version picks a route straight away ("They should acquire someone, it's fastest") without asking about timing, control or price.

Common mistakes

  • Comparing a one-off price with annual costs over different periods.
  • Ignoring the deadline: a cheap option that arrives late is not an option.
  • Forgetting execution: an acquisition the client cannot integrate may be the riskiest route of all.

Practise it

1. A bank wants a mobile payments app within six months. Building takes eighteen months. Which routes are left, and what would you ask next?

Show the answer

Partner or buy. Next, ask whether payments are core to the bank's strategy (if so, lean towards buying), what suitable targets would cost, and whether a partner would share customer data.

2. Building costs $1M upfront and $200,000 a year. Partnering costs $500,000 a year. Over how many years is building cheaper?

Show the answer

Building saves $500,000 − $200,000 = $300,000 a year against partnering, so it recovers the $1M upfront in $1M ÷ $300,000 ≈ 3.3 years. Over a horizon longer than about 3.3 years, building is cheaper, if timing allows.

Where to practise next

Try HelioVet (enter Poland directly or through a distributor?) or Stonebridge Tiles (distributors or an in-house sales team?).
